l: Chemmis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Chemmis, a Memphis king after Remphis, reigned fifty years and built Egypt's greatest pyramid, the Great Pyramid.

l: the pyramids of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: include the Great Pyramid [three principal pyramids] The pyramids stood toward Libya, one hundred and twenty furlongs from Memphis and forty-five from the Nile, and were counted among the seven wonders of the world. The text emphasizes their enormous size, costly labor, durable construction, and disputed origins, while saying that the three last kings built additional pyramids for their wives.

l: the Great Pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: requires_labor three hundred and sixty thousand men [over nearly twenty years] The Great Pyramid was attributed to Chemmis and had a square base measuring seven hundred feet on each side and a height of more than six hundred feet. It was built of solid marble, reportedly with three hundred and sixty thousand workers over nearly twenty years, and its laborers' herbs and onions were said to have cost more than sixteen hundred talents.

l: the second pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The second pyramid was built by Cephres, or according to some by his son Chabryis, in imitation of the first. It resembled the Great Pyramid in structure and workmanship but was considerably smaller, with each side of its base measuring one furlong.

l: Mycerinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mycerinus, also called Cherinus, succeeded the builder of the Great Pyramid and began a third pyramid, but died before it was completed. The text portrays him as a gentle ruler who sought his subjects' love, honored the gods, and aided people whom he judged to have been wronged in court.

l: the third pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The third pyramid was begun by Mycerinus and had a base measuring three hundred feet on each side. Its lower fifteen stories were of black marble like that of Thebes, while the remainder used the same stone as the other pyramids; it was unfinished when Mycerinus died.

l: Sabacos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sabacos, an Ethiopian king, exceeded his predecessors in worship of the gods and kindness to his subjects. He replaced death sentences with forced labor, then abdicated and returned to Ethiopia after refusing to kill the priests as directed by repeated dreams.

l: the twelve kings of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: build the twelve kings' joint tomb [as a common sepulchre] After Sabacos's departure and a two-year anarchy, twelve chief nobles of Egypt swore an oath, made laws, and jointly assumed royal power. They ruled amicably for fifteen years and began a grand common sepulchre, but all except Psammetichus later lost their sovereignty.

l: Phoenicians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Phoenicians were merchants and colonizers who learned letters and writing from Syrians. They founded Gades and its temple to Hercules, settled Malta and Gaulus, and established colonies in Africa, Sardinia, Sicily, nearby islands, and western Europe. Allegedly buying Iberian silver cheaply, they transported it to Greece, Asia, and other nations, gained great wealth, and some storm-driven merchants discovered Madeira beyond the pillars of Hercules.

l: Caria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Caria is a place adjoining Chersonesus. It was associated with Chersonesus and partly ruled by Cyrnus after his settlement, then Triopas built Triopium and gained Chersonesus and adjoining country. Later its coastal Grecian cities revolted, and Cimon stormed remaining cities, bringing Caria under his power.

l: Psammetichus's mercenary army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_composed_of Greeks [among other foreign soldiers] Psammetichus hired soldiers from Arabia, Caria, and Ionia, and used them to defeat the other kings near Moniemphis. He rewarded these mercenaries generously, settled them at Stratopedon near the mouth of Pelusium, and relied on them in governing Egypt.

l: the Egyptian soldiers who migrated to Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: More than two hundred thousand Egyptian soldiers revolted when Psammetichus favored foreign troops, rejected recall, marched into Ethiopia, and settled there, declaring their arms and fertility would secure a new country and families.

l: the Egyptian revolt and migration to Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The revolt began when Psammetichus dishonored the native Egyptian soldiers by assigning them the less favored position in an army serving in Syria. The migrants resisted the king's appeals, entered Ethiopia, and divided a rich and fruitful territory among themselves.

l: foreign trade in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Under Psammetichus, Egypt encouraged Phoenician and Greek trade, gaining wealth, foreign influence, and safe conduct for visitors.

l: Egyptian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian laws are remarkable ancient institutions, admired by Grecians especially by learned men, and said to have preserved Egyptian prosperity and order. They regulate kings, royal schedules, diet, sacrifices, occupations, taxation, courts, crimes, military conduct, commerce, theft, marriage, education, medicine, lending, and repayment. They require livelihood reports, protect debtors from imprisonment, and use rewards and punishments to promote temperance, virtue, honesty, and obedience. They also govern religious observance, burial, and the dead. The account ends by attributing written laws to Menes, who claimed to receive them from Mercury.

l: Egyptian monarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptian monarchy was presented as legally constrained rather than arbitrary. The king could not conduct public business, punish, or condemn anyone for personal reasons, but was required to follow the law in each case.

l: king (the reigning Egyptian king), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The reigning Egyptian king, attended day and night and bound by law to a daily regimen, reads letters, sacrifices, keeps appointed times, lives moderately, and rules justly with restrained appetites and punishments.

l: royal daily regimen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Royal daily regimen begins with morning correspondence, washing, dressing, and sacrifices, continues through public business, justice, air and bathing, and extends into prescribed nighttime duties.

l: royal sacrifices, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Royal sacrifices offer victims to Egyptian gods: high priest prays for the king's health, prosperity, and virtues; king views entrails, completes sacrifice; priests read records.

l: Egyptian royal diet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: limits wine consumption [to a measured quantity] The Egyptian royal diet consisted of plain foods such as veal and goose, with wine limited to a measured quantity. The diet was intended to preserve health without overcharging the stomach or causing drunkenness.

l: Egyptian royal funerals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: include mourning for a deceased king [after every king's death] At an Egyptian royal funeral, the coffin and enclosed body were placed at the entrance to the sepulchre. The king's actions were publicly rehearsed, anyone was permitted to accuse him, and the priests praised his noble deeds; a king who had ruled badly might receive no funeral pomp or solemn burial.

l: mourning for a deceased king, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lasts seventy-two days [after the king's death] After a king's death, Egyptians generally mourned for seventy-two days by tearing their garments, closing temples, stopping sacrifices and feasts, casting dust on their heads, and wearing linen girdles. They abstained from flesh, baked or heated food, wine, baths, ointments, luxurious beds, and women, while groups sang mournful songs praising the deceased king twice each day.

l: Egyptian social and economic classes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian society comprised priests, king, soldiers, shepherds, husbandmen, and artificers; soldiers formed a territorial portion, husbandmen rented land, shepherds cared for inherited flocks, and occupations generally remained inherited.

l: Egyptian soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian soldiers held a major portion of the country for military service, with allotments meant to reward service and encourage families. They obeyed the king’s expeditions, faced disgrace for desertion, mutiny, or revealing secrets, and could regain trust through valour.

l: Egyptian artificers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_restricted_to Egyptian trades [one lawful trade inherited from parents] Egyptian artificers were required to remain in the occupation allowed and taught by their parents. They were punished if they interfered in civil affairs or practiced more than one trade at a time.

l: Egyptian trades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_inherited parents [by artificers] Egyptian trades were organized by inherited occupation so that artificers could devote themselves fully to improving their crafts. The text also describes skill in agriculture, animal keeping, poultry, and geese, including the artificial hatching of young birds.

l: Egyptian courts of justice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian courts of justice were intended to punish offenders and relieve the injured without allowing money, favor, or affection to alter the law. Judges were chosen from the most reputable men of Heliopolis, Thebes, and Memphis, forming an assembly of thirty.

l: Egyptian judges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: number thirty [in the judicial assembly] Egyptian judges received salaries from the king and considered the written allegations and responses of both parties before deciding a case. They were expected to avoid the influence of lawyers' rhetoric, emotional appeals, and deceptive speech.

l: president of the Egyptian judges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The president of the Egyptian judges, chosen as the most eminent of thirty and replaceable by another judge, presided over cases wearing a golden truth emblem, which he turned toward the successful party.

l: Egyptian legal procedure, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian legal procedure uses detailed written pleadings, with plaintiff and defendant answering each point through reply and rejoinder before judges deliberate and the president indicates judgment.

l: eight books of Egyptian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_presented_to Egyptian judges [before judgment] The eight books of Egyptian laws were placed before the judges when a case was heard. They contained the laws that guided the judges' consideration of the written claims and responses.

l: written pleadings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_exchanged_by plaintiff [through reply and rejoinder] Written pleadings stated the injury, its manner, and the value of the damages, while the opposing party denied, justified, or sought to mitigate the claim. Their use was intended to prevent skilled orators and emotional speeches from gaining an advantage over less eloquent litigants.

l: Egyptian physicians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: use prescribed receipts [medicines prescribed by ancient physicians and approved by experience] Egyptian physicians receive a public stipend and use medical receipts prescribed by law and approved through the experience of ancient physicians. They are not blamed when patients cannot be cured with those receipts, but they are to suffer death if they use other medicines.

l: Egyptian common people, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptian common people are trained from childhood by parents or kindred in arts and trades by which they can earn their livelihood. Few are taught to read and write, although tradesmen especially learn both.

l: Egyptian education, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian education is provided by priests for youth in sacred and ordinary learning, emphasizing long study of arithmetic and geometry; common people learn practical arts and trades, not customarily wrestling or music.

l: Egyptian astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_studied_by Egyptian priests [through long-term observation of celestial motions] Egyptian astrologers observe the courses, motions, periods, and stops of the planets and preserve observations of the stars for many years. They claim to foresee events such as famine, disease, earthquakes, inundations, and comets, and the text says that the Chaldeans learned their reputation in astrology from Egyptian priests.

l: Egyptian medicine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian medicine prevents or treats disease through legally prescribed clysters, purging potions, abstinence, and vomits, relying on remedies selected through long experience as effective.

l: theft in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: requires_owner_payment_of a fourth part of the value [as redemption for recovered stolen goods] In Egypt, registered thieves are to give their names to a chief and deliver to him whatever they steal. Owners of lost goods report the details of the loss in writing; after the stolen goods are valued, the owner pays one-fourth of the value to recover them.

l: Egyptian marriage customs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian marriage customs permit priests one wife and other Egyptians multiple wives, require raising as many children as possible, and recognize bond-maid children as legitimate.

l: Egyptian capital punishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian capital punishment is a body of penalties for offenses including perjury, failing to rescue or report a threatened victim, false accusation, unjust livelihood, murder, and parricide. Penalties can mirror the threatened punishment or involve death, while parricide is punished by mangling, thorns, and burning. Execution of pregnant women is delayed until delivery. Some offenses receive nonfatal punishments: parents who kill children must embrace their bodies for three days and nights, and military secret revelation brings tongue-cutting or degradation.

l: murder, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes killing a bond slave [when done wilfully] A person who wilfully kills a freeman or a bond slave is to die under Egyptian law. Parents who kill their children are not executed but are forced to hold them continually for three days and nights, while convicted parricides are mangled and burned alive.

l: debt and lending, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Debt and lending rules free a borrower who, under oath, denies an unwritten loan. Written loans may charge interest only up to double the principal. Collection reaches only the debtor’s goods, not the debtor’s body, which remains available to the city for public service.

l: adoration and worshipping of beasts among the Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A religious practice among the Egyptians, it honors sacred animals in life and after death through dedicated land, care, ensigns, and lamented burial; it is explained by animals' usefulness, military representations, and stories of divine transformation.

l: sacred animals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sacred animals are fed, cared for, honored, and buried by the Egyptians. Killing one is punishable by death, while killing a cat or the bird ibis can provoke a mob to kill the offender even without a formal trial.

l: cats, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sacred animal [especially protected in Egypt] Cats are fed bread soaked in milk and fish, stroked, honored, and buried by the Egyptians. A Roman was killed by an Egyptian mob after accidentally killing a cat, and cats are also said to protect people from serpents and asps.

l: dogs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sacred animal [in Egypt] Dogs are worshipped and mourned by the Egyptians; when a dog dies in a house, the whole family shaves its body and laments. Dogs are valued for guarding houses and assisting in hunting, and Anubis is represented with a dog's head.

l: Apis worship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_based_on Osiris [according to Egyptian explanations] Apis worship involves treating the sacred ox as a god and maintaining a costly household for him. The Egyptians explain this worship by saying that the soul of Osiris enters one ox after another, while other accounts connect Apis with the members of Osiris.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Italy is a region and land traversed by Hercules after Gaul and the Alps, including Liguria, Tuscany, Rome’s region, and maritime coasts; it contains the Tiber, where Hercules camped, and lies above the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is presented as a source of migration to Sicily and Liparus’s flight, and as the home of the Tyrrhenians, whose institutions and architecture influenced the Romans. Its fertile Campania flourished, while Tarentines founded Heraclea after expelling Siris’s inhabitants. Later, Dionysius sought power in Italy through wars involving Lucanians, Thurians, and Greek cities.

l: worship of the crocodile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_based_on protection [according to one Egyptian explanation] The worship of the crocodile is explained as a response to the creature’s supposed protective value, to Menas’s rescue, or to the general Egyptian practice of honoring creatures believed to have secured human safety. The text also connects such worship with gratitude and with the division of religious customs among different Egyptian regions.

l: Egyptian religious divisions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: prevents Egyptians [from agreeing among themselves] One account says that a prudent ancient ruler divided Egypt into regions and assigned each region the worship of a particular beast or prohibited particular foods. This division allegedly prevented the Egyptians from uniting in rebellion, since each region honored its own creature and slighted the religious practices of others.

l: Egyptian funerary customs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian funerary customs honor the deceased through burial and praise. Friends and kindred mourn until interment by throwing dirt, running through the city, and abstaining; funerals range from magnificent to inexpensive, ending in burial in tombs, apartments, or houses.

l: mummification, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mummification preserves and scents a body: it is opened on the left side, intestines are removed while kidneys and heart remain, bowels are washed with wine and spices, then cedar oil and ointments treat it for forty days before myrrh and cinnamon rubbing and return to the family.

l: the deceased, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The deceased is prepared for burial and may be accused of having lived badly before the coffin is placed on the ship. If no valid accusation is made, the deceased is praised for education, piety toward the gods, justice toward people, chastity, and other virtues, and is prayed into the company of the just.

l: friends and kindred of the deceased, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: announces the funerary judgment [by declaring the day of the lake crossing] The friends and kindred mourn publicly, abstain from comforts, and arrange the manner and expense of the funeral. They announce the funeral to judges and others, praise the deceased when no accusation succeeds, and may later redeem the body of an ancestor by paying debts or securing absolution.

l: Egyptian funeral workers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian funeral workers inherit ancestral mummification and burial arts, provide written funeral costs, and divide tasks: a scribe marks an incision, a cursed Paraschistes cuts, and honored Taricheutae cleanse internal organs.

l: the forty judges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A funerary tribunal of forty judges assembles beyond the lake, hears accusations against the deceased, punishes malicious false accusers, and decides burial eligibility.

l: Charon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Charon, called a ferryman in the Egyptian country language, pilots and governs a funerary ship carrying the dead across a lake in a ceremony Orpheus saw.

l: the funerary judgment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A funerary judgment before the coffin boards a ship permits accusations of evil life; proven charges deny ordinary burial, while false or malicious accusers face severe punishment.

l: the lake crossing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: uses ship [piloted by Charon] The lake crossing takes place after the forty judges assemble and a ship is brought to the shore by its pilot. The relatives announce that the deceased is to pass across the lake, and the crossing follows the funerary judgment.

l: Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Jupiter Triphylius is presented as Saturn’s son, a king and conqueror who succeeded and defeated Saturn, ruled the world, punished the impious, benefited mankind, and treated subjects justly and courteously; they therefore called him Father. After death he was placed in the highest heavens, worshipped as the chiefest god and supreme lord, and called Zeus or Zena for teaching men proper living. He fathers Hercules through Alcmena after taking Amphitryon’s shape and lengthening the night, declares the day’s child king of the Persians, arranges Hercules’s immortality through twelve labours, orders him to obey Eurystheus, and later calls him an Olympian god. He imprisons Prometheus, strikes Salmoneus and Asclepius, purifies Ixion, and fathers Aeacus by Aegina. His temple in Panchsea is greatly revered, and Panara’s citizens call themselves his suppliants.

l: virtue and honesty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptian customs described are said to promote virtue, honesty, faithful dealing, and orderly conduct by making rewards and punishments visible in ordinary life and burial practices. The text contrasts this with Greek stories about the just and impious, which it claims were treated as invented fables and did not reform behavior as effectively.

l: Egyptian legislators, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: established written laws The Egyptian legislators are said to have created laws governing public life, religious worship, military discipline, royal administration, contracts, and provincial government. Their laws were highly praised, although many were later abrogated by the Macedonians.

l: Menes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Menes is an Egyptian legislator, heroic and famous for a commendable life, who first instituted written laws in Egypt, claiming Mercury gave laws meant to greatly benefit the public.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lacedaemonians are a Spartan people, polity, and state, repeatedly presented as a military power acting with confederates and allies in struggles over Athens, Persia, Greek cities, and control of the sea. Early, fewer than five hundred with the Thespians remain under Leonidas to defend the straits and die fighting. They later join the defense of Attica, fight Persian forces at Plataea, oppose Athens’s fortification, and seek to restrain Athenian power. They fight Helots and Messenians at Ithome, reject Persian proposals to attack Athens, support and enlarge Thebes as a counterweight to Athens, and enter the Peloponnesian war against Athens. Their campaigns include invasions of Attica, naval losses to Phormio, the siege and destruction of Plataea, operations around Pylos, Brasidas’s campaigns, victory near Amphipolis, and a peace restoring captured cities. They continue wars and alliances, aid Syracuse, occupy Decelea, seek Persian assistance, and endure naval reverses. Rebuilding fleets under Lysander and Callicratides, they ultimately blockade Athens and compel its subjection. Afterward they hold sovereign command over Greece by sea and land, establish oligarchies, impose tribute, and support garrisons and governors. Their supremacy is then contested: they aid Cyrus, fight Persians and a confederacy including Boeotians and Athenians, lose command of the sea after Cnidus, and make further efforts to recover it. Wearied by war against Grecians and Persians, they send Antalcidas to Artaxerxes, accept imposed peace terms, and cease fighting.

l: Sasychis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sasychis, the second Egyptian law-maker, was a wise and prudent prince who added laws on honoring and worshiping the gods, discovered geometry, and taught astronomy.

l: Olympic games, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hercules instituted the Olympic Games near the river Alpheus in Elis, dedicated the place to Jupiter Olympus, and established horse-coursing, wrestling, and other contests announced to cities by messengers. In one Olympiad Synouris was added. Later Dionysius displayed chariots, tents, and singers; spectators turned from admiration to ridicule, rifling tents as chariots crashed or left the course.

l: Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Samos is an island whose history centers on shifting alliances, conflict, and democracy. It sent ambassadors seeking aid for Asia’s inhabitants; Greek commanders returned there after battle and accepted Ionians and Eolians as confederates. Pericles first reduced Samos and established democracy. A later opposing faction, aided by Persians, seized it, but Pericles besieged and captured it, demolished its walls, removed its ships, and restored democracy. Later, forces assembled there and received Samian ships before sailing to Arginusae.

l: Melampus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Melampus, a soothsayer and son of Amythaon, restored Argos’s women to sanity after Bacchus drove them mad, then received a third of Argos and ruled it with Bias.

l: Cerberus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cerberus was the dog of hell. Hercules brought him up from the infernal regions tied in his chain and presented him to open view.

l: Helen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Helen, the daughter of Jupiter and Leda, was about ten years old and of surpassing beauty when Perithous and Theseus seized her at Lacedaemon. The two men carried her to Athens and cast lots for her, with Helen falling to Theseus. Theseus kept her secretly at Aphidna under the care of Aethra and other friends, but Castor and Pollux later captured Aphidna, carried Helen away to Lacedaemon, and took Aethra captive with her. Helen was still a virgin when she was recovered.

l: Theodorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Theodorus, Rhoecus's son, made part of Apollo Pythius at Ephesus, governed Athens, held great noble authority, and urged removing Dionysius to restore laws and liberties.

l: Ephesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ephesus is a military base in Asia. It repeatedly serves as a gathering, command, departure, and retreat point: Lysander assembles and sails a fleet, Thimbron and Dercyllidas station forces, and Agesilaus gathers troops, begins his campaign, and returns with his army.

l: Assyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Assyrians were a long-ruling Asian group that fought in Ninus’s conquests and under Sardanapalus against revolting Medes, Persians, Babylonians, and allies. After an early defeat by Bactrians, they prevailed through numbers; later, despite early victories, they were defeated near Nineveh and the Euphrates.

l: Book II, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Historical book by Diodorus Siculus covering ancient Asia, beginning with the Assyrian empire and early conquests of Ninus and Semiramis.

l: Ninus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ninus, the first recorded king of Assyria, is warlike and ambitious for honour and glory. He allies with Arieus, conquers neighboring peoples and broad Asian territory, builds Nineveh, marries Semiramis during the Bactrian expedition, and fathers Ninyas. After his death, Semiramis becomes regent.

l: Babylonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: call Jupiter (Belus) [Belus] The Babylonians call the Chaldeans their most ancient people and assign them a distinguished religious and civic position.

l: Armenia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_governed_by Teribazus [as lord-lieutenant of the Persian king] The Greeks crossed the river Centrites into Armenia, which was governed by Teribazus for the king. They initially passed through the province under an agreement of friendship but then endured severe winter conditions in the Armenian mountains.

l: Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nineveh was a great city near the Euphrates, built by Ninus and named after him, the capital of the Assyrian empire and seat of Sardanapalus. Inhabited chiefly by wealthy Assyrians and also other nations, it had vast dimensions, strong walls, plentiful supplies, and fifteen hundred turrets. Confederates besieged it for three years; the Euphrates broke its wall, after which they entered, dispersed inhabitants, restored estates, and razed it when the Medes ruined the Assyrian empire.

l: Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Bactria is a strong, wealthy country with many large, populous cities and a principal city of the same name. Oxyartes mustered four hundred thousand men before Ninus subdued the province and seized its wealth. Later Semiramis gathered her army there and sent boats overland toward the Indus.

l: Semiramis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Semiramis is a queen of Assyria, portrayed as exceptionally beautiful, intelligent, courageous, able, and ambitious. Raised by Simma and named from pigeons, she first marries Menon and has Hypates and Hydaspeas. She helps capture Bactria, becomes Ninus’s wife, bears Ninyas, buries Ninus, and rules as queen regent. Seeking to surpass earlier rulers, she governs Asia except India for forty-two of her sixty-two years and directs Babylon’s construction and many works across Asia. Her Indian invasion ends in defeat and wounding; after her son’s assault, she yields the crown and disappears.

l: Menon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Menon, a high officer governing Syria and commanding Thessalians, marries Semiramis but hangs himself after Ninus demands she be given to the king.

l: Ninyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ninyas, son of Ninus and Semiramis, became ruler after Semiramis, who had first retained the kingdom as his regent. He reigned peaceably, unlike Semiramis avoiding valour and martial affairs, living secluded in his palace, and ruling through annually changed provincial armies and governors.

l: Medes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Medes supplied forces under Arbaces, joined Persians and other allies in revolt against Sardanapalus, invaded and overthrew the Assyrian empire. They then conquered Assyrians and ruled an expanding empire until Cyrus conquered Astyages. Later, as Persian troops at Thermopylae, they led the attack but were defeated by Leonidas's Greek formation with heavy losses.

l: laws and courts of justice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Law and justice are attributed to Saturn, Themis, Ceres, and Jupiter in different ways. Saturn promoted integrity, Themis taught laws and sacred order, Ceres was said to establish rules for truthful dealings, and Jupiter instituted punishment for injuries and the orderly settlement of disputes in courts.

l: Nineveh's construction, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ninus built Nineveh near the Euphrates after his earlier conquests. The city had a long circuit of four hundred and fourscore furlongs, walls a hundred feet high, broad ramparts, and fifteen hundred high towers.

l: Ninus's conquest of Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes Egypt [among the coastal and adjoining countries overrun] Ninus conquered Babylon, Armenia, Media, Egypt, Phoenicia, Coelosyria, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Lycia, Caria, Phrygia, Mysia, Lydia, and many other countries. He subdued nearly all of Asia between the Tanais and the Nile within seventeen years, except the Indians and Bactrians.

l: Ninus's invasion of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After an earlier unsuccessful attempt, Ninus invaded Bactria with an army said by Ctesias to include seventeen hundred thousand foot, over two hundred and ten thousand horse, and ten thousand six hundred hooked chariots. He divided the army because of the narrow and difficult passages.

l: siege of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ninus's forces defeated the Bactrians in the open country and subdued their other forts and castles, but the city of Bactria resisted because of its strength and provisions. The siege continued until Semiramis identified a neglected route to the citadel.

l: capture of Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Semiramis led men over the rocks, crossed a deep trench, and seized part of Bactria's castle. After she signaled the attackers, the defenders panicked, abandoned the walls, and the city was taken.

l: Semiramis's accession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_from Menon's death [after Menon hanged himself] Semiramis rose to royal power after Menon hanged himself when he refused to surrender her to Ninus. After Ninus died, she became queen regent and held the kingdom for their son Ninyas.

l: Ninus's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ninus dies after returning from Bactria and settling provincial affairs; Semiramis buries him beneath a huge mound in the royal palace and rules as regent.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Syracuse is a Greek city, called the greatest among the Grecians, containing Ortygia, Epipolae, a great haven, and forts. It is associated with Arethusa and Cyane, and its inhabitants observed annual ceremonies for Ceres and Proserpine. Its political life moved between civic rule and domination: Gelon returned from Himera as benefactor, king, and deliverer; Hiero ruled; citizens expelled Thrasybulus and restored democracy, followed by three hundred years of peace and prosperity until Dionysius. The city also endured disputes over mercenaries, land, faction, Petalism, and tyranny, while its assembly at times protected suppliants such as Deucetius and decided questions of war, prisoners, and government. Syracuse directed campaigns, received refugees and displaced inhabitants, and became a center of resistance after Agrigentum fell. Its most prominent danger was siege: Athenians attacked by land and sea after taking Epipolae, but Syracuse, aided by Gylippus, Corinth, and Lacedaemon, destroyed their works, won on land and sea, celebrated safety, and debated mercy toward prisoners. Under Dionysius, fear and division enabled absolute authority; he strengthened defenses, separated the fortified island, controlled weapons, recruited foreign troops, and made the city a center for arms, ships, and engines. Carthaginian attacks damaged its harbor and later besieged it with forts, yet its citizens fought at sea, captured supplies, and helped destroy the opposing fleet. Syracuse remained outside Carthaginian control and became a base for Dionysius's expeditions into Italy.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hannibal was a Carthaginian general, chief magistrate of Carthage, and grandson of Amilcar. Appointed to lead an expedition to Sicily, he raised mercenaries in Spain, recruited citizens and Africans, equipped a fleet, and commanded an invasion army supplied by transport ships. He captured and destroyed Selinus, then besieged and razed Himera in revenge for his family’s earlier defeat, burning its temples and returning to Carthage with abundant booty. Later, as general with full authority over the war, he sailed with fifty galleys after the naval defeat at Eryx to aid the army’s transport. Commanding a siege with Amilcar, he ordered monuments and tombs destroyed for siege mounds, and died in a plague among the Carthaginian army.

l: city (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Babylon is a city in the province of Babylon, built around the Euphrates, which runs through its middle; walls surround it with 200 feet of open space before the houses, and a bridge connects across the river.

l: city wall (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Babylon’s wall surrounds the city, built of brick cemented with brimstone. It extends 360 furlongs, though others give 365, with 250 stately turrets, great height and breadth, space from houses, morass defenses, and room for six chariots abreast.

l: bridge (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A bridge over the Euphrates, built by Semiramis at its narrowest part, spans five furlongs and is thirty feet wide. Stone pillars, spaced twelve feet apart, support it; iron hooks, lead, pointed current defenses, and cedar, cypress, and palm flooring complete it.

l: palaces of Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The palaces of Babylon are two palaces at opposite ends of the bridge, one on each side of the Euphrates, overlooking the city. Built by Semiramis, they were richly decorated with walls, creatures, hunting scenes, statues, and armies, and connected by a vault beneath the river. They later decayed or were greatly damaged.

l: hanging garden (Babylon), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The hanging garden near the citadel, a 400-foot-square garden, was built by Cyrus rather than Semiramis for a Persian courtesan. It rises through masonry-supported arches and planted terraces, irrigated by Euphrates water drawn through conduits, conveyances, and engines.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyrus is presented as a Persian ruler and prince whose records combine accounts of conquest, rule, rebellion, and death. As king of Persia and the most powerful prince of his age, he conquered Astyages and transferred the empire from the Medes to the Persians. Another account says that, after leading a mighty army into Scythia, he was defeated, captured, and crucified by its queen. He is also described as Darius's son and Artaxerxes's brother. Summoned into Persia, he entrusted provincial affairs to Lysander; he commanded maritime provinces, appointed kinsmen as governors and Tanios of Memphis over Ionia and Aeolia, and prepared secretly to wage war against Artaxerxes. With Lacedaemonian aid, Greek mercenaries, and Asian troops, he assembled at Sardis, crossed the Euphrates toward Babylon, and concealed his purpose until gradually revealing it and raising pay to prevent desertion. In battle he struck Artaxerxes with a javelin but was mortally wounded by a common Persian soldier. His death frightened his army, prompted the Greeks to retreat, and ended the expedition in defeat.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Persia is an empire that came to hold Babylon after Cyrus conquered Astyages and transferred the Medes’ empire to the Persians. It expanded power over Greek cities in Asia and threatened Greece through Xerxes’ invasion, demanding earth and water and mounting a vast land and naval expedition. After Persian defeats, it agreed to free the Greek cities in Asia. Succession trouble followed Xerxes’ death, but Artaxerxes restored order, answered revolt in Egypt, sought coastal control, opposed the Lacedaemonians, and intervened against Evagoras in Cyprus.

l: building of Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The building of Babylon is a grand, costly construction project using architects, artists, materials, and two million workers from across the empire. It builds walls, a bridge, embankments, palaces, a river passage, and Jupiter Belus's temple, before much later decays.

l: Ecbatana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ecbatana is a city on a low, even plain, initially lacking a nearby spring; Semiramis built a palace there and supplied abundant water by canal from a mere beyond Mount Orontes.

l: Ethiopian burial customs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes throwing dead into the Nile [regarded by some as the best burial] Ethiopian groups use several forms of burial: some cast the dead into the river, some preserve them in houses by covering them with melted glass, and some bury them in earthen coffins near temples. Swearing by the names of the buried is considered a sacred oath.

l: Stabrobates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Stabrobates was king of India and commanded immense forces, many elephants, river-boats, and an army larger than Semiramis's. He challenged Semiramis, defeated her army, wounded her in battle, and stopped pursuing her after prodigies and the advice of soothsayers.

l: Indian campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian campaign is an unprovoked undertaking against India. Semiramis gathered men, arms, and transportable boats in Bactria; after a naval victory including the Battle of the Indus, Indian elephants defeated the Assyrian army.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indus is a very large, swift river running from the north into the ocean. It borders and divides India from the rest of Asia, receives navigable rivers including Hipanis, Hydaspes, and Arcesinea, and is second only to the Nile in size. During Semiramis's invasion, fleets and armies fought, captured places, and crossed it by boat bridge.

l: Cyprus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyprus is an island and a contested theater of power. Cimon and the Athenians defeat a Persian fleet, capture several cities, bring most of the island under Athenian control, and leave Salamis under a Persian garrison as Cimon dies there. Later, Evagoras, king of Salamis, expands his authority, prompting other cities to seek Artaxerxes’ aid and making Cyprus the scene of war.

l: Indian elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian elephants are described as the largest, strongest, and most courageous elephants, numerous and heavily equipped for war. Captured, trained, and maintained by the king, they carry one calf after sixteen to eighteen months and suckle it for six years. In battle, they terrified enemies, destroyed mock elephants, trampled and tore apart soldiers, and helped defeat the Assyrian army.

l: mock elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Three hundred thousand mock elephants were made from black oxen skins and straw, each carrying men and a camel. They initially deceived Indian scouts and frightened horses from afar, but real Indian elephants exposed and destroyed them.

l: Assyrian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Assyrian army included millions of infantry, hundreds of thousands of cavalry and chariots, camel-mounted soldiers, boats, and mock elephants. It initially advanced successfully but fled when the Indian elephants attacked, suffering severe losses while retreating across the bridge of boats.

l: Indian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has Indian elephants [in greater number and fully armoured] The Indian army was larger than Semiramis's and included many well-armored elephants, cavalry, chariots, infantry, and river-boats. After being deceived by the mock elephants, it recovered, attacked the Assyrian army, and forced it to retreat.

l: bridge of boats, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: crosses Indus [built by Semiramis from boats] Semiramis constructed a broad bridge of boats over the Indus and crossed it with most of her forces, leaving sixty thousand soldiers to guard it. During the retreat she ordered its cords and tenons cut, causing many Indians on the boats to drown and securing her escape.

l: Battle of the Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Battle of the Indus began with a naval victory by Semiramis, who sank a thousand Indian vessels and captured prisoners. After crossing the river, Assyrian forces were routed by Indian elephants; Stabrobates wounded Semiramis, who fled.

l: Semiramis's disappearance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Semiramis's disappearance follows Ninyas's treacherous plot and a eunuch's assault. Remembering an oracle, she yields the crown and commands obedience to her son, then vanishes, interpreted as translation to the gods; some accounts say she became a dove.

l: Sardanapalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sardanapalus, the thirtieth king from Ninus and last king of the Assyrians, surpasses his predecessors in sloth, luxury, and sensuality. After Arbaces defeats his forces and besieges Nineveh, he burns himself, treasure, eunuchs, and concubines in the palace court.

l: Arbaces the Mede, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arbaces the Mede, a valiant and prudent general, is persuaded to challenge the Assyrian empire. He unites several forces, endures defeats and a wound, defeats Sardanapalus’s forces after Nineveh falls, becomes king, and rules Media.

l: Belesis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Belesis, a Babylonian Chaldean priest famed for astrology and divination, persuades Arbaces to revolt and sustains conspirators with predictions of success. After secretly taking Sardanapalus’s treasure, he receives and retains Babylon’s government when Arbaces pardons him and grants the treasure.

l: Priam, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Priam, son of Laomedon and brother of Hesione, is characterized by justice and equity. When Laomedon refuses to honor his agreement with Hercules, Priam urges that Hesione and the promised horses be restored. Ignored, he secretly aids Iphiclus and Telamon and exposes Laomedon’s plan. After Hercules takes Troy, he makes Priam king. Priam rules Troy, marries Hecuba, and has many sons, including Hector, noted for valor in the Trojan War.

l: Paphlagonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: contains Cotyora [Cotyora is a Greek colony there] Paphlagonia was selected as the direction of the Greek march toward the sea. The Greeks later passed through areas associated with Paphlagonia and its neighboring regions.

l: revolt against Sardanapalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The revolt, led by Arbaces and Belesis with allied provincial forces, gathers four hundred thousand soldiers, suffers three defeats, gains the Bactrian army, defeats Sardanapalus's forces, and besieges Nineveh.

l: siege of Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lasts two years [before the river breach in the third year] The siege of Nineveh lasted two years without decisive success because of the city's strong walls and the limited siege technology of the age. In the third year, the overflowing Euphrates breached twenty furlongs of wall, allowing the besiegers to enter after Sardanapalus's death.

l: overthrow of the Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by revolt against Sardanapalus [after the capture of Nineveh] The Assyrian empire was overthrown after Arbaces's confederates defeated its forces and captured Nineveh. Arbaces was proclaimed king, appointed governors over the provinces, and transferred the remaining royal treasure to Ecbatana.

l: gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The gods are said to have been born among the Atlantides, according to their report. Several human rulers and benefactors, including Uranus, Titea, Helios, Selene, and Cybele, are said to have been honored as gods after their deaths or notable deeds.

l: planets, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Five stars called Interpreters by the Chaldeans are identified as planets; moving through twelve zodiac signs, they are said to influence human nativities and future events, though they are not visible at sea near Arabia in following months.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Artaxerxes is repeatedly presented as king of Persia and Asia, ruling the Persians with justice and equity for forty years. His rise began in violence: persuaded by Artabanus, he killed his brother Darius and took the throne; when Artabanus later attacked him, he defended himself, killed Artabanus, and secured his kingship. After the death of Xerxes, he punished those involved in his father's murder, reorganized government, stored provisions, and prepared forces. He faced revolt in Egypt, raising a fleet and sending armies under Archemenes, then Artabazus and Megabyzus. Warned of his brother Cyrus's conspiracy, he assembled a vast army, marched against him, was wounded, but recovered as his forces defeated Cyrus and his army. He punished captured Greek commanders, rewarded loyal soldiers, and entrusted coastal governments and later commands to Tissaphernes, Tithraustes, and Struthius. After Persian setbacks in Cyprus and conflict with the Greeks, he accepted peace: Greek cities in Asia were to return to obedience, while other Greeks governed by their own laws. Free from that war, he prepared for war against Evagoras in Cyprus, ordering ships and aid for opponents of Evagoras.

l: Cadusians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cadusians, a nation famed for independence, were led by Parsodes in revolt against the Medes, defeated a Median army, made him king, and remained Median enemies until Cyrus transferred empire to the Persians.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Amazons are a warrior nation of women and virgins, centered at Themiscyra on the Thermodon, with martial government, training, and religious festivals and sacrifices for Mars and Diana. They conquer neighboring peoples and large parts of Europe and Asia, and are celebrated as valiant warriors. They ally with Bacchus against the Titans and, in another account, are commanded by Minerva. After refusing Hercules’s demand for Hippolyta’s belt, they are attacked near Themiscyra: many leaders are killed, queen Melanippe is defeated, and the nation is said to be destroyed. The survivors assemble at Thermodon, ally with the Scythians, march through the Cimmerian Bosphorus into Attica, encamp at Amazonian Field, and are defeated by Theseus; those remaining go into Scythia as the nation gradually becomes extinct.

l: Hyperboreans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: inhabit Hyperborean island [beyond the northern breezes] The Hyperboreans inhabited an island in the ocean beyond Gaul and the north wind. They were described as prosperous people with a temperate climate, a special friendship for the Greeks, and a religious devotion to Apollo.

l: Great Ocean, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The ocean lies beyond the pillars of Hercules and contains the remote island described as Madeira. Phoenician merchants entered it after sailing beyond the pillars and were driven into it by a violent storm for many days before reaching the island.

l: Gandarides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gandarides are a group east of the Ganges, renowned for breeding multitudes of monstrous war elephants; their four thousand elephants deterred Alexander, leaving them unconquered by any foreign king.

l: India's inhabitants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: India’s inhabitants are described as numerous, skilled, healthy, long-lived, and divided into seven ranks. They are said to have developed their arts gradually and to have laws regulating occupations, marriage, government, agriculture, and justice.

l: Indian philosophers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian philosophers are the first, least numerous, and most esteemed social rank, free from public offices. They perform sacrifices and funerals, annually predict natural events in public assemblies, advise people, and lose public speaking rights after incorrect predictions.

l: Indian husbandmen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian husbandmen, the second social rank, cultivate fields while living there with families. Regarded as serving the common good, armies spare them in war; they pay kings tribute from produce and do not privately own land.

l: Indian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian kings are described as owning all the land and receiving tribute, including a fourth part of agricultural produce. They maintain the soldiers, war-horses, and elephants from the treasury, and select counselors, governors, judges, and generals from the senators.

l: Indian rivers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian rivers descend from the northern mountains, water the plains, and enrich the country with gardens and fruit. The philosophers and naturalists explain their abundance by saying that rain flows down from the higher neighboring countries.

l: Indian agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: produces two harvests annually [winter and summer harvests] Indian agriculture produces two crops each year, including wheat, rice, millet, sesamus, pulse, and a crop called Bosphorus. Rivers, summer rains, naturally growing fruits, and edible marsh roots provide additional food.

l: famine in India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_absent India [according to the account, because of two harvests and abundant natural produce] The text says that India never experiences famine or a shortage of provisions because the land yields two abundant harvests and also supplies naturally growing fruits and marsh roots. Laws protecting husbandmen from wartime devastation are said to help prevent famine.

l: Indian social ranks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_number seven [covering almost all India] The people of India are divided into seven ranks: philosophers, husbandmen, herdsmen and shepherds, mechanics, the militia, ephori, and senators. Marriage and occupations are generally restricted to the rank into which a person was born.

l: Indian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Indian laws describe a quadrangular India and regulate war, social ranks, marriage, occupations, and strangers. They protect husbandmen during war, prohibit servitude while requiring equal respect for free people, yet restrict marriage and work to one’s tribe and inherited calling.

l: Bacchus's conquest of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a conquest [attributed to Bacchus by Indian accounts] Bacchus is said to have entered India from the west with a large army when its inhabitants lived scattered and its cities were unable to resist him. After a plague weakened his soldiers, he moved them to the mountains, recovered them there, and later conquered and organized the country.

l: Alexander's invasion of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a invasion [Alexander reached the Ganges but did not conquer Gandarides] During Alexander’s invasion of India, he conquered the Indians behind him and advanced as far as the Ganges. He did not attack the Gandarides after learning of their four thousand war elephants.

l: Scythian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Scythian empire, a vast and glorious empire, grew from a small tract through warfare and conquest, eventually extending to the Caucasus, ocean, Maeotis, Tanais, Caspian Sea, Nile, and beyond.

l: Sauromatians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sauromatians were people drawn from Media and settled near the Tanais by Scythian kings; after growing numerous and powerful, they devastated Scythia, destroyed conquered peoples, and brought ruin to the Scythian nation.

l: Thermodon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The river Thermodon was the setting of a powerful nation governed by female queens. The city of Themiscyra was built at its mouth.

l: Amazon queen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: An Amazon queen governs and leads military campaigns, trains women, subdues neighbors, establishes martial laws, founds Themiscyra, and is called daughter of Mars after successes.

l: Themiscyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [with a stately palace] Themiscyra was a large city built by an Amazon queen at the mouth of the river Thermodon. It was beautified with a stately palace.

l: Diana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Diana is a goddess, closely associated with Dictynna and sometimes identified as the same person. Medea claimed Diana came from the Hyperboreans in a dragon-drawn chariot to preserve Pelias and his city and establish her worship. She was honored in Crete and associated with Ephesus, Pontus, Persia, and other places.

l: Eurystheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Eurystheus is king of Argos and king of Mycenae, brought forth before his full time through Juno's intervention. He commands Hercules to perform twelve labours, including killing the Nemean lion; he imposes the tenth task, driving away Gerion's oxen, because he thinks it too great for Hercules, and later orders Hercules to bring Cerberus from hell. Terrified by Hercules' return with the Erymanthian boar, he later banishes Hercules and others from the kingdom. Fearing the Heraclidae will expel him, he orders their banishment from Greece and leads an army against them. They rout his forces, and Hyllus kills him after his chariot breaks during flight; his sons also fall.

l: Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Amazon queen Hippolyte was an Amazon queen whom Hercules was ordered to fight. Hercules captured her and took her belt.

l: Penthesilea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amazon queen and daughter of Mars, she aided Trojans and killed many Greeks before Achilles slew her during the Trojan War.

l: Hector, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a son of Priam and Hecuba [especially valiant in the Trojan War] Hector was the son of Priam and Hecuba. He was especially remarkable for his valor in the Trojan War.

l: Achilles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands Trojan War [with Agamemnon] Achilles was the son of Peleus and Thetis. He went with Agamemnon to the Trojan War and killed Memnon.

l: Hyperborean island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hyperborean island is an island opposite Gaul under the Arctic pole, as large as Sicily, with rich soil, temperate climate, two annual crops, Apollo’s sacred grove, round temple, and consecrated city.

l: Apollo's temple, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Apollo's temple on the Hyperborean island was described as a renowned, round structure beautified with many rich gifts. Sacred hymns praising Apollo were sung there by harpers.

l: Delos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: holds common fund [for public service of the allied cities] Delos was selected as the location of a common treasury where money collected for public service would be kept. Under Aristides's administration, the contributions reached 560 talents.

l: Scythian conquest and expansion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Scythians expanded from the area near the Araxes across the mountains to Caucasus, the plains toward the ocean and lake Maeotis, and the plain to the Tanais. Their descendants later conquered territories beyond the Tanais and extended their power toward Egypt, the eastern ocean, the Caspian Sea, and lake Maeotis.

l: Amazon wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Amazons conquered neighboring nations and extended their wars into Europe and Asia. Their wars eventually weakened them after Hercules defeated them, and surrounding peoples continued attacking them until their nation disappeared.

l: Hercules's expedition against the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a military expedition [ordered by Eurystheus to obtain Hippolyte's belt] Hercules undertook an expedition against the Amazons at the command of Eurystheus. He routed them in battle and took Hippolyte and her belt, after which the Amazons became vulnerable to attacks from neighboring peoples.

l: Amazons' extinction, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_from Amazon wars [following Hercules's victory and later attacks] After Hercules's victory, the Amazons were repeatedly attacked and greatly reduced. Following Penthesilea's death, their nation grew weaker until it was wholly extinct, and later ages regarded their earlier exploits as fictions and fables.

l: Hyperborean religion and Apollo worship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Hyperboreans worshipped Apollo above all other gods and honored him with songs, sacrifices, and sacred ceremonies. Their city contained harpers who sang hymns about his glorious acts, and their island had a sacred grove and temple dedicated to him.

l: Arabia the Desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arabia the Desert is a barren and dry region with little fruit, especially in the country inhabited by the Nabatheans. It contains hidden wells, a fortified rock, and a large brimstone-producing mere, while its watered areas support palm-trees and balsam.

l: Nabatheans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Nabatheans inhabit a partly desert, waterless eastern country where little land bears fruit. They roam to conduct incursions and robberies, use secret wells for refuge, remain free without a foreign prince, and were never conquered by Assyrians, Medes, Persians, or Macedonians.

l: Taprobane, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Taprobane is an island, also called Ceylon or Zeilao, identified in scripture as Ophir according to Bochart.

l: Lambulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lambulus, learned from youth, became a merchant after his father’s death. Captured in Arabia and used in the Ethiopian purification, he reached an island, lived there seven years with a fellow-captive, was expelled, reached Greece, and wrote of his adventures and India.

l: the fortunate island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_inhabitants gentle and kind people The fortunate island was the destination prescribed by the Ethiopian oracle for the two strangers. It was said to contain gentle and kind people with whom the strangers could live happily.

l: the seven islands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The seven islands are equal in size and spacing, share laws and customs, and unfold as naturally abundant places supplying their inhabitants with plentiful provisions.

l: the island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A round island, five thousand furlongs around, lies under the equator. It has equal days and nights, no noon shadow, a moderate climate, a rough tidal sea of fresh water, and many unusual plants, animals, and springs.

l: the islanders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The islanders are unusually shaped people over four cubits tall, with flexible bones, limited hair, and generally healthy 150-year lives. They courteously provision Lambulus and his companion, then appear as scientifically and astrologically skilled tribes practicing subsistence work, worship, and communal child-rearing.

l: the Ethiopian purification, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Ethiopian purification purges Ethiopia’s land and nation by sacrificing, crowning, and sending two stranger ritual purifiers south toward a fortunate island with provisions, under severe punishment for returning early.

l: the voyage to the island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lambulus and his fellow-captive sail directly south, endure storms and hardships for four months before reaching the island, then depart and sail more than four months to India.

l: the ship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A small seaworthy vessel, manageable by two men, carries Lambulus and his companion with six months’ provisions. Prepared by Ethiopians after their seven-year stay on an island, it is fitted out for their departure.

l: the island's inhabitants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: receive Lambulus [courteously] The island's inhabitants were more than four cubits tall and had flexible bones, tender bodies, strong nerves, little body hair, wide ear openings, and divided tongues. Their tongues enabled them to imitate birds and speak simultaneously to two people. They lived long lives, often reaching one hundred and fifty years, and welcomed the arriving strangers.

l: the island societies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The island societies are distinct kin-based groups of at most four hundred members, governed by the eldest under the island's king; members rotate occupations and public offices until old age.

l: the islanders' laws and customs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: requires_execution_of the infirm [those who are lame or otherwise weak] The islanders killed people who were lame or otherwise physically infirm, and individuals who reached the legally appointed age ended their lives by lying on a special herb. They did not marry, shared women, raised children communally, wrote downward from the top of the page, followed prescribed diets, worshiped the heavens and celestial bodies, and buried their dead at the seashore.

l: the healing animals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Small tortoise-like animals have four eyes and mouths but share one throat and digestive system; their blood instantly heals living wounds and, while fresh, restores severed nonvital limbs.

l: the island's natural abundance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: produces corn [without cultivation and more than enough] The island's fertile soil and temperate air caused grain, fruits, vines, olive trees, calamus, cotton-bearing reeds, and other useful growths to flourish. The inhabitants obtained abundant food, oil, wine, clothing materials, sweet springs, hot and cold baths, and harmless serpents whose flesh they ate.

l: Ethiopian letters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ethiopian letters are an image-based writing system used by Ethiopians, representing beasts, body parts, tools, and other objects; their symbolic meanings are learned through continual use and practice rather than syllabic combinations.

l: Ethiopian laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: prohibits execution of subjects [even when the subject is guilty] Ethiopian laws regulate royal selection, punishment, the conduct of kings, relations between kings and household servants, and funerary matters. They require rulers to govern according to ancient customs and forbid subjects from being directly put to death, instead sending them a sign that leads them to kill themselves.

l: Ethiopian religion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ethiopian religion is described as claiming first institution of worship, sacrifices, and festivals; Ethiopians consider their sacrifices especially acceptable, worship Isis, Pan, Hercules, and Jupiter, and some regard the sun, moon, and universe as eternal.

l: Ethiopian kingship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_based_on divine selection [the king is selected when the carried god first lays hold of him] Among the Ethiopians near Meroe, priests select a king from among their ranks according to which candidate is first seized by a carried deity, and the people then worship him as a god. Other Ethiopian peoples choose kings for beauty, wealth, courage, or industrious care for subjects.

l: gold mining and refining, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gold mining and refining in Egypt requires much labour: workers soften hard earth and rock with fire, break it with pickaxes and hammers, pound and grind it, then wash the powder with water to remove earthy and drossy matter. The gold is washed repeatedly, cleaned with sponges, weighed, and refined for five days and nights in clay-sealed earthen urns in a furnace with lead, salt, tin, and barley bran.

l: Ethiopian priests, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ethiopian priests, consecrated officials devoted to purity and religion, shave, dress distinctively, carry sceptres, and elect kings. At Meroe they command kings to die until Ergamenes rejects them and kills them.

l: Ethiopian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: governs_by Ethiopian laws [rewards and punishments follow ancient laws] Ethiopian kings are expected to rule according to ancient laws and customs and traditionally receive divine honors. Their household servants are said to imitate any bodily maiming of the king and to kill themselves when the king dies; Ergamenes was the notable king who abolished the priests' authority to command royal suicide.

l: gold, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gold is a material found naturally pure and unrefined in Arabian hollows, and dug from white shining veins in black soil or collected from Gaulish rivers. It is crushed and washed so its weight retains it while earth runs off, then purified with sponges and heat in sealed earthen pots into slightly lighter pure gold. Mining and refining bring toil and vexation; gold becomes ornaments and temple scatterings.

l: gold mines (Egypt, Arabia, and Ethiopia), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gold mines are a rich mining region in the confines of Egypt and neighbouring Arabia and Ethiopia, where vast labor digs gold from dark, winding workings through naturally black soil, white veins, gold-bearing rock, and other bright metals.

l: kings of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: condemn_to condemned workers (the gold mines) [for work in the mines] The kings of Egypt condemn notorious criminals, captives taken in war, persons sometimes falsely accused, and people against whom a king is incensed to labor in the mines. Sometimes the condemned people's kindred and relations are sent with them so that their labor may increase the king's profit and gain.

l: labourers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Labourers in the mines soften rock, break it into pieces, carry it out, pound it with iron pestles, and grind it in mills. They work continually under the overseer's direction and may be driven with lashes or blows.

l: condemned workers (the gold mines), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The condemned workers are forced labourers in the mines, including criminals, captives, falsely accused people, offenders against the king, and some relatives. Bound in fetters and poorly clothed, they continually break rock with hammers, pickaxes, and forehead lamps. Even sick, injured, old, or infirm workers are driven on, and many die.

l: barbarian guards, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Barbarian soldiers of various and strange languages strictly guard condemned workers in the gold mines, as language differences prevent workers from corrupting or persuading them.

l: forced labour and punishment in the mines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: uses fire [to soften the hardest earth and gold-bearing material] The mines use forced labor as both punishment and a means of advancing the king's profit. Workers are kept in fetters, denied rest, strictly guarded, and compelled to continue through lashes and cudgelling until some collapse and die.

l: rock, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: contains gold [hardest rock is worked for gold] The hardest gold-bearing rock is softened by fire and broken with iron pickaxes and hammers. Workers follow the bright vein rather than undermining the rock in a direct line, then pound and grind the extracted pieces until they become fine meal.

l: tin, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tin is found in rocky ground in Belerium, mixed with veins of earth. Inhabitants melt and refine it, shape it into four-square pieces, carry it by carts at low tide to Ictis, and merchants transport it through France toward the mouth of the river Rhone.

l: Ichthyophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Ichthyophages are nations dispersed along sea-coasts from Carmania and Gedrosia to the far end of the Red sea, including the Arabian gulf. They live chiefly by catching and eating fish, shellfish, and other sea creatures, build shelters from whale ribs covered with sea-grass, and preserve an ancient account of the gulf once lying dry and green before water returned.

l: Troglodytes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Troglodytes are a pastoral people, including communities called Nomades, living in tribes under monarchs. They move between pastures, feed on milk, blood, and meat from old or sick cattle, wear beast skins around the loins, and share wives and children except for the monarch’s wife. They practice circumcision except among those called cripples, fight over grazing pastures, and bind and stone the dead in burial. They also kill the helpless or incurably ill, hunt wild beasts, prize the wild bull’s strength, and occupy a coast near Ethiopia beside the Arabian gulf as far as deserts.

l: Ichthyophages' sea-coast communities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ichthyophages' sea-coast communities are groups living in shore caves, cliffs, and rocky valleys. Their customary subsistence centers on trapping fish with stone-blocked passages, gathering catches together, and processing fish by drying, boiling, or mixing it with Paliurus seed; fish bones serve as emergency food and other uses.

l: fish, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Fish are brought inland by the tide and become trapped among the stone barriers and hollows when the water recedes. The people collect, sun-dry, boil, and mix them with Paliurus seed, while also eating some fish raw during periods when fishing is difficult.

l: tide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: occurs twice daily [about the third and ninth hour] The tide flows in and covers the shore twice each day, around the third and ninth hour. It carries fish into the coastal hollows, and when it ebbs the water leaves the fish exposed and unable to escape.

l: sea-coast fishing and food-processing practices, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: use goat horns and rough stones [as fishing and cutting implements] The Ichthyophages use natural coastal passages and heaps of stones as fish traps, catching smaller fish by hand and larger creatures with goat horns or broken stones.
