They sun-fry their catch in stone pots, remove the flesh from the bones, boil it with Paliurus seed, and dry the resulting mass on tiles.

l: whales, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: provide_food_for Cetivores [when cast up by the sea] Whales are cast up by the sea and provide food for the Cetivores. When stranded whales are unavailable, the Cetivores are reduced to gnawing old, foul-smelling bones and sucking the ends of rotten ribs.

l: Chelonophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a tortoise-eating people The Chelonophages inhabit small, low, barren islands near the continent and live by capturing sea-tortoises. They fry the tortoises in the sun and use their shells as boats and as roofs for their cottages.

l: sea-tortoises, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sea-tortoises feed underwater at night and rise during the day to sleep at the surface with their shells erect. The Chelonophages swim quietly toward them, turn them onto their backs, guide them to shore, and tow them with ropes.

l: Chelonophages' islands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: shelter sea-tortoises [from storms and tempests] The islands are numerous, small, low, and barren in both cultivated land and natural produce. Because they lie close together, their promontories break the force of the waves and create calm waters where sea-tortoises gather.

l: Cetivores, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Cetivores are whale-eating people on the continental shore near the Chelonophages, living on cast-up whales and suffering near-starvation when none are available.

l: whale-eating, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Whale-eating provides the Cetivores with abundant food when stranded whales are plentiful. During shortages, they eat pieces of decayed whale bones and suck the rotten ribs.

l: fish traps of the Babylonian coast, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The inhabitants construct reed and cane barriers along the shore, with small portals that open as the tide enters and close as it withdraws. Fish pass through with the incoming water but are left behind when the tide ebbs, allowing the inhabitants to gather them or trap them in channels leading to their cottages.

l: Rizophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rizophages are root-eating people in Ethiopia above Egypt near the Asa, peacefully thriving on prepared cane roots in marshes, yet often attacked by lions outside them.

l: cane roots, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Rizophages dig up cane roots, wash them, bruise and pound them with stones, and broil handfuls of them in the sun. These roots constitute the food on which they live.

l: lions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lions leave deserts for watered champaign country and the Rizophages’ land, seeking shelter, pasture, and prey; they tear apart unarmed Rizophages until swarms of gnats drive them away.

l: Spermatophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Spermatophages are a nation that gathers and feeds on plentiful fallen fruit in summer, then eats a sweet, turnip-stalked herb growing in shady valleys during the rest of the year.

l: elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Elephants are wild beasts among the southern parts of Troglodyta. When full after feeding, they sleep leaning against trees and cannot rise if they fall on their backs. Elephantophages hamstring or fell them by cutting trees, then kill and eat them; Ethiopians’ serpents also blind, coil around, and tear them apart. Ptolemy the Second collected and trained many for war.

l: Simoes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a nation [Ethiopian] The Simoes inhabit the country west of the Elephantophages and attack the Struthophages. They are also described as neighboring Ethiopians who use the horns of Oryxes as weapons.

l: Struthophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a nation The Struthophages live south of the Simoes and hunt the large birds found in their country. They use the birds' flesh for food and their skins for clothing and bed coverings, and defend themselves against the Simoes with Oryx horns.

l: Hylopliages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hylopliages are a nation of slender, light-bodied people who, with wives and children, climb and move among trees like birds, feeding on buds and tender branches. They wear no clothing, share wives and children, fight with clubs, and sometimes are furnished to death when blindness prevents food-gathering.

l: Ethiopian Hylogones, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ethiopian Hylogones are a few hunters who sleep in trees to avoid wild beasts, ambush animals at water pools, kill them with clubs, stones, and darts, and train boys in archery through withheld food.

l: Elephantophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: An Ethiopian nation dwelling in large wooded forests, Elephantophages watch elephants from treetops, then hunt them by clinging to tails and cutting hind-leg sinews with sharp axes or by felling trees against which they sleep.

l: Struthophages' bird, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Struthophages' bird is a large bird partly resembling a beast, with a long neck, round body, wings, small head, strong thighs and legs, and forked feathers. Flightless but swift-running, it uses wind to move and throws stones from its feet; low wind makes it easily caught.

l: Acridophages, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Acridophages live near the deserts and depend on locusts for food. They trap the locusts with smoke and fire, salt their bodies for preservation, and are described as small, lean, black, swift, and short-lived people.

l: locusts, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_driven_by south winds [in spring] Locusts are driven from the desert by south winds in spring and fall into a valley where the Acridophages burn combustible materials. The smoke kills them, after which the Acridophages collect and salt them, preserving them as food for the rest of the year.

l: spiders and scorpions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Spiders and scorpions multiplied greatly in a formerly inhabited country after an excessive rain. Their bites and stings immediately killed people, forcing the inhabitants to abandon the country.

l: Cynomones, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cynomones, called wild Ethiopians by neighboring barbarians, inhabit the southern border, keeping fierce dogs to hunt entering beasts, especially Indian oxen, and living mainly on meat.

l: Cynomones' dogs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: hunts Indian oxen [in large numbers] The Cynomones' dogs are fierce hunting animals used to pursue Indian oxen and other beasts. The Cynomones release them against herds that they cannot otherwise master.

l: Indian oxen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: visits Cynomones [from the beginning of the summer solstice to midwinter] Indian oxen enter the country of the Cynomones in innumerable numbers from the beginning of the summer solstice to the middle of winter. Their reason for migrating is unknown, and the Cynomones hunt them with dogs, eating some fresh and salting others.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rhodes is an island, later also a city formed by incorporating inhabitants from Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus. It was first inhabited by the Telchines, then associated with Rhode, and consecrated to Sol after Sol dried its primordial moisture and cleared the Telchines’ flood. Before Tlepolemus arrived, Hellenes inhabited it; a colony led by Triopas also settled there. Tlepolemus divided the island into three parts and founded Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus, while remaining sons of Sol built Achaia and dwelt at Ialysia. Later, Rhodes refused the Peloponnesian fleet, revolted from the Lacedaemonians, received Conon, and helped seize grain ships. It then defected from Athens amid factional conflict, expulsions, and a siege involving Rhodian exiles.

l: Alexandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_destination_of capture of the thirty-cubit serpent Alexandria was the destination to which the huntsmen brought the captured thirty-cubit serpent. The serpent was presented to Ptolemy the Second there and became a remarkable sight for visitors to his kingdom.

l: Rhinoceros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Rhinoceros is a beast bred in Ethiopia, nearly equal to elephants in courage and strength but shorter. With very hard, ox-colored skin and a flat iron-hard horn sharpened on stones, it fights elephants over pasture by goring beneath the belly.

l: pastoral life of the Troglodytes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The pastoral life of the Troglodytes consists of moving between pastures with their flocks and living chiefly on cattle products and meat. During rainy periods they consume boiled milk mixed with blood, and when pastures are burned by the sun they move to low marshes and sometimes fight for suitable grazing.

l: serpents, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Serpents near Ethiopian deserts are reported as incredibly large; hundred-cubit claims are rejected, but a thirty-cubit serpent was captured and taken alive to Alexandria, while Ethiopians say giant serpents can overpower elephants.

l: huntsmen, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The huntsmen hunt beasts skillfully and, encouraged by Ptolemy the Second, undertake bringing a thirty-cubit serpent alive to Alexandria. An attempt kills two; they then drive it with horses, dogs, darts, slingers, and noise into a net.

l: Ptolemy's elephant-hunting expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ptolemy's elephant-hunting expedition involved encouraging skilled hunters with great rewards and assembling many elephants for training in war. The expedition also led to strange beasts becoming known to the Grecians and provided the context for the hunt for the giant serpent.

l: capture of the thirty-cubit serpent, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The capture of a thirty-cubit serpent began after huntsmen found it in standing pools. Two men died in a direct attempt; hunters then blocked its den, used a bulrush net, and drove it in with men, horsemen, dogs, weapons, and trumpets to bring it to Alexandria.

l: taming of the serpent, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: makes_tame serpents [by keeping the serpent low and short of food] After the serpent was brought to Alexandria, it was kept short of food until its fierceness diminished. It gradually became very gentle, and Ptolemy the Second kept and fed it as a spectacle for visitors.

l: Syrtes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Macs, described as the most populous of the groups mentioned, inhabit areas near the Syrtes. Air apparitions are also said to occur in the region near the Syrtes.

l: frankincense, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: comes_from frankincense tree [distilling from the bark after incision] Frankincense grows abundantly on the Holy Island and is used for the worship of the gods throughout the world. It comes from a small tree whose bark yields drops like tears when cut.

l: Carmutha, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Carmutha is a famously described port beneath a large promontory, with a wide entrance, capacity for two thousand ships, fresh water, and a garden-suitable harbor island; it resembles Cothon in commodiousness and harbor design.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Carthage is a city in Africa, a political and military center repeatedly shaped by war, diplomacy, celebration, disaster, and recovery. It agreed with Xerxes to attack Greeks in Italy and Sicily while he invaded Greece, then spent three years raising a vast army and fleet. Its Sicilian expedition was defeated at Himera, bringing fear and mourning, but its ambassadors obtained peace from Gelon under financial and religious conditions. Carthage later welcomed Hannibal with public acclamation after his successes in Sicily, answered Syracusan peace envoys doubtfully, and renewed preparations for operations there with armies, warships, and transports. It received Agrigentum's choicest spoils, including the Phalarian bull, though the bull was later found there when the city was destroyed and restored to the Agrigentines. Alarmed by Dionysius's demands amid plague and poor preparation, it also served as Himiico's departure point and as refuge after defeat. Finally threatened by African rebels, it used ceremonies, sacrifices, naval preparation, and Sardinian supplies until the rebel army dispersed.

l: Peloponnesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Peloponnesians are a people inhabiting the Peloponnese, hosted by Debse because of Hercules's ancient familiarity with the nation. They sought security by favoring defense near the isthmus and helping build a wall from Lechaeum to Cenchreae. In later fighting, they served in the Lacedaemonian fleet and suffered defeats near Cyzicum and Claros, but also won actions near Mitylene. Under Lysander, they defeated the Athenian fleet, captured Sestos, and helped blockade Athens until it surrendered.

l: Sabeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sabeans are the most populous Arabian people, inhabiting wealthy Arabia the Happy. Exceptionally rich through high-priced trade, they remain unconquered; their hereditary kings cannot leave the palace, or an ancient oracle requires the people to stone them.

l: myrrh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Myrrh comes from myrrh tree roots when earth is dug; on Holy Island, rich-soil trees produce deep red spring myrrh and white later myrrh twice a year.

l: Saba, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a capital city [of the Sabeans; situated on a high hill] Saba is the capital city of the Sabeans and stands on a high hill. It is the royal seat, where vessels, cups, beds, chairs, household goods, buildings, and temples are richly adorned with gold, silver, ivory, precious stones, and other costly materials.

l: Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyrene is described as having fat, very fertile soil. It produces corn, wine, oil, fruit, and pasture, and is watered by many rivers. Cyrene suffered a great civil conflict after Aristocrates and others seized the city and five hundred leading citizens were suddenly killed. Its exiles joined the Messenians in attacking the city, and the Cyrenians later ended their internal conflict by swearing to forget past injuries.

l: Libyan raiders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Libyan raiders, a third sort of Libyans, wear goat skins and continually live by spoil and robbery, recognizing neither king nor obligation as they raid from deserts, steal, and retreat to hiding places.

l: the southern Libyan desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The southern Libyan desert is a barren, waterless region, like a featureless sea, with long sand stretches, scarce life, and many venomous serpents.

l: sand, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sand forms extensive heaps across the inland desert and makes the Cerestes difficult to see because they are the same color as the ground. People may step on them unknowingly and risk losing their lives.

l: serpents, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: abound_in the southern Libyan desert [in great numbers] The desert contains serpents of many shapes and sizes, whose bites are described as mortal. They are especially numerous in the barren sandy regions and are reported to have once devastated much of Egypt.

l: Cerestes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cerestes are mortal-biting serpents, sand-colored and hard to distinguish from ground, so they may be stepped on accidentally.

l: air apparitions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Air apparitions are airy images in desert regions near the Syrtes, especially in calm weather, resembling large living creatures. They appear to stand, move, fly, or pursue people; their frightening effect on strangers can bring coldness and trembling.

l: Amazons of Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Amazons of Africa were an ancient nation ruled by women, who held warfare and public authority while men managed domestic affairs and raised children. Armed with swords, darts, bows, and serpent-skin armor, they built Chersonesus, conquered the Atlantides, fought neighboring Gorgons, and expanded through Africa and Asia. After defeats by Mompsus and Sipylus, survivors withdrew into Libya; Hercules extirpated them.

l: Gorgons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gorgons were a powerful African nation of women, enemies of the Amazons who troubled the Atlantides; Merina captured many, Perseus conquered them under Medusa, and Hercules extirpated them.

l: Tritonis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tritonis was a morass near the ocean and the island of Hisperia, bordered by Ethiopia and associated with the river Triton. The Amazons built the city of Chersonesus in it, but an earthquake later opened the tract toward the ocean and swallowed up the entire morass.

l: Mount Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a mountain [the greatest mountain in those parts] Atlas was the name the Grecians gave to the greatest mountain in the region bordering the Tritonis morass and extending to the ocean. The Amazons attacked the people living upon Mount Atlas, who possessed a rich country with many cities.

l: Atlantides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Atlantides are inhabitants of a rich country near Mount Atlas, bordering the ocean, noted for surpassing neighbors in receiving and entertaining strangers. Initially defeated by Merina and the Amazons, they submitted after Cercene’s destruction, surrendered their cities, formed a league with Merina, and honored her with rich gifts. They also preserve a genealogy of the gods, claiming the gods were born among them.

l: Merina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Merina, queen of the Amazons of Africa, commands a large army, conquers the Atlantides and Gorgons, overruns parts of Africa and Asia, builds cities including Merina after Cercene’s destruction, and consecrates Samothracia after a storm. She is killed battling Mompsus and Sipylus; remaining Amazons succeed her in defeat.

l: Phrygia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Phrygia is said to be the birthplace of Cybele. Its inhabitants report that Mæones ruled Phrygia and Lydia, that Cybele was exposed on Mount Cybelus, and that the Phrygians later established her worship at Pessinunte.

l: Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mitylene is a city built around an old city on a small island and a later mainland addition. Though an exception among Lesbos’s cities in remaining loyal to Athens, its people revolted and the Athenians besieged it; famine forced surrender, the inhabitants were spared, and its walls demolished. Later, it held an Athenian garrison, endured another siege, and was relieved after Arginusae.

l: great mother of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The great mother of the gods had sacred mysteries that were taught by Electra to Jasion and later brought into Asia by Dardanus, Cybele, and Corybas. Corybas gave his name to those who celebrated these rites in a state of religious frenzy.

l: Samothracia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Samothracia, a sacred island consecrated to the mother of the gods, was formerly called Samos, received its later name from colonies from Samos and Thrace, and preserves ancient speech, religious traditions, flood associations, Saon, and sacred mysteries.
